quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: 'Whereas' compares two different things directly — not one thing changing over time.
quests.explanation: Clause 1 (The north office focuses on sales) + 'whereas' + clause 2 (the south office handles support). 'Whereas' contrasts two separate facts side by side.
quests.textToSpeak: The north office focuses on sales, whereas the south office handles support.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: Here 'while' means 'although' or 'whereas' — it isn't describing two things happening at once.
quests.explanation: 'While' + contrast (some team members prefer remote work) + main clause (others miss the office). 'While' can introduce a contrast, not just simultaneous time.
quests.textToSpeak: While some team members prefer remote work, others miss the office.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: Two contrasting personality traits are compared directly by 'whereas'.
quests.explanation: Clause 1 (He tends to overthink decisions) + 'whereas' + clause 2 (his partner acts quickly). 'Whereas' often highlights a difference between two people or things.
quests.textToSpeak: He tends to overthink decisions, whereas his partner acts quickly.

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: 'Both' and 'and' work as a matched pair, framing two qualities together.
quests.explanation: Subject (The proposal) + verb (was) + 'both' + adjective 1 (ambitious) + 'and' + adjective 2 (realistic). 'Both...and' links two qualities as equally true.
quests.textToSpeak: The proposal was both ambitious and realistic.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: 'Either' and 'or' also pair up, presenting two alternative choices.
quests.explanation: Subject (We) + 'can' + 'either' + option 1 (upgrade the system) + 'or' + option 2 (replace it entirely). 'Either...or' presents two possible choices.
quests.textToSpeak: We can either upgrade the system or replace it entirely.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: 'Neither...nor' negates both subjects together — nobody saw it coming.
quests.explanation: 'Neither' + subject 1 (the manager) + 'nor' + subject 2 (the team) + verb (anticipated) + object (the delay). 'Neither...nor' negates two subjects at the same time.
quests.textToSpeak: Neither the manager nor the team anticipated the delay.

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: Two matching 'the + comparative' clauses balance each other — as one grows, so does the other.
quests.explanation: 'The more' + clause 1 (data we collect) + ',' + 'the clearer' + clause 2 (the pattern becomes). This paired structure shows two things increasing together.
quests.textToSpeak: The more data we collect, the clearer the pattern becomes.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: This time the second half decreases instead of increasing, but the pattern is the same.
quests.explanation: 'The longer' + clause 1 (the meeting ran) + ',' + 'the less productive' + clause 2 (it felt). 'The more...the less' shows one thing rising while another falls.
quests.textToSpeak: The longer the meeting ran, the less productive it felt.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: A short, simple version of the same structure — still two matching halves.
quests.explanation: 'The sooner' + clause 1 (we start) + ',' + 'the easier' + clause 2 (this will be). Even short clauses can use this paired comparative structure.
quests.textToSpeak: The sooner we start, the easier this will be.

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: 'It could be argued that' softens a claim, distancing the speaker slightly from a strong opinion.
quests.explanation: 'It could be argued that' + embedded clause (the results are still preliminary). This hedge presents an opinion cautiously, without stating it as fact.
quests.textToSpeak: It could be argued that the results are still preliminary.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: 'Appears to' softens the claim, and 'though not conclusively' adds a further limit at the end.
quests.explanation: Subject (This evidence) + 'appears to' + verb (support) + object (this theory) + 'though not conclusively'. 'Appears to' hedges a claim, and the final phrase limits how strong that claim really is.
quests.textToSpeak: This evidence appears to support this theory, though not conclusively.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: 'One might question whether' is a formal, hedged way of raising doubt.
quests.explanation: 'One might question whether' + embedded clause (the sample size was large enough). 'One' here means 'a person in general', common in formal academic hedging.
quests.textToSpeak: One might question whether the sample size was large enough.

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: The phrase between the commas simply renames 'Dr. Patel' with her role.
quests.explanation: Subject (Dr. Patel) + appositive (', the lead researcher,') + verb (will present) + object (the findings) + time (tomorrow). An appositive renames the subject without needing 'who is'.
quests.textToSpeak: Dr. Patel, the lead researcher, will present the findings tomorrow.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: The middle phrase explains exactly what the prototype is, before the sentence continues.
quests.explanation: Subject (Our prototype) + appositive (', an early version of the final product,') + verb (failed) + object (the first test). The appositive gives background information about the subject.
quests.textToSpeak: Our prototype, an early version of the final product, failed the first test.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: The appositive identifies the supplier's location, tucked neatly between commas.
quests.explanation: Subject (Our supplier) + appositive (', a company based in Vietnam,') + verb (raised) + object (its prices). This appositive adds useful context without a separate sentence.
quests.textToSpeak: Our supplier, a company based in Vietnam, raised its prices.

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: 'Did' stresses that the action really happened, defending against doubt.
quests.explanation: Subject (I) + 'did' (emphasis) + base verb (send) + object (the invoice) + ';' + result (it must have gotten lost). Emphatic 'did' confirms an action strongly, often when someone doubts it happened.
quests.textToSpeak: I did send the invoice; it must have gotten lost.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: 'Does' adds emphasis to the present tense verb, insisting the understanding is real.
quests.explanation: Subject (She) + 'does' (emphasis) + base verb (understand) + object (the risks) + 'even if she seems calm'. Emphatic 'does' strengthens a present-tense claim against doubt.
quests.textToSpeak: She does understand the risks, even if she seems calm.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: 'Did warn' insists the warning genuinely happened, despite what followed.
quests.explanation: Subject (We) + 'did' (emphasis) + base verb (warn) + object (them) + 'but' + clause 2 (they proceeded anyway). Emphatic 'did' defends a past action's truth before contrasting it with the outcome.
quests.textToSpeak: We did warn them, but they proceeded anyway.

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: One subject performs three actions in a row, joined by commas and a final 'and'.
quests.explanation: Subject (He) + verb 1 (reviewed the contract) + verb 2 (flagged two issues) + 'and' + verb 3 (sent it back). A single subject can carry three coordinated actions using commas and a final 'and'.
quests.textToSpeak: He reviewed the contract, flagged two issues, and sent it back.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: The three actions happen in a clear sequence, even though only 'and' marks the connection.
quests.explanation: Subject (She) + verb 1 (opened the store) + verb 2 (restocked the shelves) + 'and' + verb 3 (greeted the first customers). Listing three actions in order implies they happened in that sequence.
quests.textToSpeak: She opened the store, restocked the shelves, and greeted the first customers.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: Each of the three verbs keeps its own object, even though the subject only appears once.
quests.explanation: Subject (Our team) + verb 1 + object 1 (gathered the data) + verb 2 + object 2 (ran the analysis) + 'and' + verb 3 + object 3 (shared the results). Each coordinated verb can carry its own separate object.
quests.textToSpeak: Our team gathered the data, ran the analysis, and shared the results.

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: 'Frankly' interrupts the sentence briefly, adding the speaker's honest tone.
quests.explanation: Subject (Our results) + inserted word (', frankly,') + verb (were) + adjective (disappointing). A single adverb set off by commas can insert the speaker's attitude mid-sentence.
quests.textToSpeak: Our results, frankly, were disappointing.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: 'In theory' hints that reality might turn out differently than expected.
quests.explanation: Subject (This approach) + inserted phrase (', in theory,') + verb ('should reduce') + object (costs) + adverb (significantly). 'In theory' signals the claim is expected but not yet proven.
quests.textToSpeak: This approach, in theory, should reduce costs significantly.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: 'Understandably' briefly justifies the client's reaction before the sentence continues.
quests.explanation: Subject (That client) + inserted word (', understandably,') + verb (wants) + object (a faster response). This inserted word shows the speaker sympathizes with the subject's reaction.
quests.textToSpeak: That client, understandably, wants a faster response.

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: 'Implementation' turns the verb 'implement' into a noun, common in formal writing.
quests.explanation: Subject (The implementation of the new policy, a nominalized verb) + verb (caused) + object (some confusion). Nominalization turns an action into a noun, often sounding more formal.
quests.textToSpeak: The implementation of the new policy caused some confusion.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: 'Failure to communicate' packages an entire idea into a compact noun phrase.
quests.explanation: Subject (Their failure to communicate, a nominalized phrase) + verb phrase ('led to') + object (unnecessary delays). This turns 'they failed to communicate' into a noun phrase acting as the subject.
quests.textToSpeak: Their failure to communicate led to unnecessary delays.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: 'Rejection' nominalizes 'reject', letting the whole event act as a single subject.
quests.explanation: Subject (This rejection of the proposal, a nominalized verb) + verb (disappointed) + object (the entire team). Nominalizing 'reject' into 'rejection' lets the event itself become the grammatical subject.
quests.textToSpeak: This rejection of the proposal disappointed the entire team.

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: A contrast clause, an inserted time clause, and the main point all combine in one flowing sentence.
quests.explanation: 'Whereas' + contrast (the old system required manual updates) + subject (the new one) + inserted clause (', once configured,') + verb ('updates itself automatically'). Multiple B2 structures — contrast, insertion, and a main clause — layer together here.
quests.textToSpeak: Whereas the old system required manual updates, the new one, once configured, updates itself automatically.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: The paired comparative structure is followed by a further hedge, softening the overall claim.
quests.explanation: 'The more' + clause 1 (thoroughly we test) + ',' + 'the fewer' + clause 2 ('surprises we'll face') + 'though' + hedge (nothing can guarantee complete reliability). A paired comparative can be followed by a cautious limitation.
quests.textToSpeak: The more thoroughly we test, the fewer surprises we'll face, though nothing can guarantee complete reliability.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: A relative clause, emphatic 'did', an embedded clause, and an inserted contrast all appear together.
quests.explanation: Subject (Dr. Patel) + relative clause (', who led the original study,') + 'did eventually confirm that' (emphasis) + embedded clause ('the results, while promising, were far from conclusive', containing its own inserted contrast). This sentence combines nearly every structure introduced across this file.
quests.textToSpeak: Dr. Patel, who led the original study, did eventually confirm that the results, while promising, were far from conclusive.
